IUT4.Thm1_10Theorem 1.10Log-volume Estimates for Θ-Pilot Objects
Record

Log-volume estimates for Theta-pilot objects. For initial Theta-data in the situation of IUT III Corollary 3.12, with E_F of good reduction at the good nonarchimedean valuations not dividing 2l, the tripodal field F_tpd = F_mod(E_{F_mod}[2]), the (3 5)-torsion of E_F rational over F and F = F_mod(sqrt(-1), E_{F_mod}[2 3 5]): the real number (l+1)/(4|log(q)|) {(1 + 12 d_mod/l)(log(d^{F_tpd}) + log(f^{F_tpd})) + 10(e*_mod l + eta_prm) - (1/6)(1 - 12/l^2) log(q-frak)} - 1 may be taken as the constant C_Theta of IUT III Corollary 3.12 (that is, it is an admissible real bound in the sense of that corollary), and hence, by C_Theta >= -1, (1/6) log(q-frak) <= (1 + 20 d_mod/l)(log(d^{F_tpd}) + log(f^{F_tpd})) + 20(e*_mod l + eta_prm) <= (1 + 20 d_mod/l)(log(d^F) + log(f^F)) + 20(e*_mod l + eta_prm). Here |log(q)| = log(q-frak)/(2l).

Explicit hypotheses.

  • a collection of initial Theta-data as in IUTchI Definition 3.1, in the situation of IUTchIII Corollary 3.12
  • E_F has good reduction at every valuation in V(F)^good intersect V(F)^non that does not divide 2l
  • d_mod = [F_mod : Q]; e_mod (1 <= e_mod <= d_mod) the maximal ramification index of F_mod over Q; d*_mod = 2^12 3^3 5 d_mod, e*_mod = 2^12 3^3 5 e_mod
  • F_mod in F_tpd = F_mod(E_{F_mod}[2]) in F, the tripodal field obtained by adjoining the fields of definition of the 2-torsion of any model of E_F over F_mod
  • the (3 5)-torsion points of E_F are defined over F
  • F = F_mod(sqrt(-1), E_{F_mod}[2 3 5]) = F_tpd(sqrt(-1), E_{F_tpd}[3 5]), with E_{F_tpd} the model given by the Legendre form
  • d^{F_box}, q^{F_box}, f^{F_box} the arithmetic divisors of the different, the q-parameters at V(F_box)^bad, and the conductor, and their log-degrees as on page 23; eta_prm the positive real number of Proposition 1.6

Implicit hypotheses.

  • l is a prime >= 5 (IUTchI Definition 3.1) and l != 5 (noted on page 22 from IUTchI Definition 3.1 (c)); hence l >= 7, which the final estimate uses
  • |log(q)| > 0 is the quantity of IUTchIII Corollary 3.12, equal to log(q-frak)/(2l) (page 23)

Conclusion.

The displayed expression is an admissible value of C_Theta for IUT III Corollary 3.12, and the two-line final inequality for (1/6) log(q-frak) holds.

Obligations.

  • The local inputs (Propositions 1.1 to 1.5, 1.8), (E5), the construction of IUT III Theorem 3.11 and IUT III Corollary 3.12 are not formalized.
  • The arithmetic of the steps is checked in the fragments of the step records; the displayed value of C_Theta is the definition of the fragment IUT4.Thm1_10.frag.constant.

Ambiguities.

  • The Lean definition constant keeps |log(q)| (variable q) and log(q-frak) (variable Q) as separate arguments; the relation q = Q/(2l) of page 23 is a hypothesis of the lemmas that need it.

    Record

    To estimate C_Theta one must bound from above the procession-normalized mono-analytic log-volume of the holomorphic hull of the union of possible images of a Theta-pilot object, relative to the Kummer isomorphisms, in the multiradial representation of IUT III Theorem 3.11 (i), subject to the indeterminacies (Ind1), (Ind2), (Ind3). This is done at each v_Q in V_Q: for each j in {1, ..., l*} one bounds the component in I^Q(S^pm_{j+1}; n,o D^|-_{v_Q}) and then averages over j. Since S^pm_{j+1} = {0, 1, ..., j} and that object is a tensor product of j+1 copies of the direct sum of the Q-spans of the log-shells at the elements of V(F_mod)_{v_Q}, one bounds, for each collection {v_i}_{i in S^pm_{j+1}} of (not necessarily distinct) elements of V(F_mod)_{v_Q}, the component for the tensor product of the Q-spans of the corresponding log-shells, and then takes the weighted average over all such collections as in Remark 1.7.1.

    Explicit hypotheses.

    • the situation of Theorem 1.10 and of IUTchIII Theorem 3.11 and Corollary 3.12
    • j in {1, ..., l*}, regarded also as an element of F_l^*; S^pm_{j+1} = {0, 1, ..., j} (IUTchI Proposition 6.9 (i); IUTchIII Proposition 3.4 (ii))

    Implicit hypotheses.

    • the log-volume to be bounded is additive over v_Q in V_Q and its procession normalization is the average over j

    Conclusion.

    Reduction of the bound for C_Theta to local upper bounds: for each v_Q and each j, an upper bound for the log-volume component attached to each collection {v_i}{i in S^pm{j+1}} of elements of V(F_mod)_{v_Q}, followed by a weighted average over collections (Remark 1.7.1) and an average over j in {1, ..., l*}. IUT4.Rem1_10_1Remark 1.10.1
Record

A motivation of the series was to build a framework in which an analogue of the scheme-theoretic Hodge-Arakelov theory of [HASurI], [HASurII] avoids the obstructions to diophantine applications met there. The computation of the leading term ((l*+3)/2) log(d_{v_Q}^K) - ((2l*+1)(l*+1)/(12l)) log(q_{v_Q}) in the final display of Step (v) of the proof of Theorem 1.10, via (E1), (E2), is described as essentially identical to the computation of the leading term in the proof of [HASurI], Theorem A; the author states the computations were essentially known around 2000 and the problem was to construct a framework in which to perform them, comparing this with the Weil conjectures before Weil cohomology and with computations motivated by physics.

Explicit hypotheses.

  • the notation of Theorem 1.10 and of Step (v) of its proof

Conclusion.

An informal comparison: the leading term ((l*+3)/2) log(d_{v_Q}^K) - ((2l*+1)(l*+1)/(12l)) log(q_{v_Q}) of Step (v) arises from (E1), (E2) as in the proof of [HASurI], Theorem A. No mathematical assertion is made that needs proof.

Obligations.

  • Nothing to prove; a heuristic and historical remark.

Ambiguities.

  • Page 31: 'essentially identical' is not made precise; the corresponding computation of [HASurI] is not reproduced.

IUT4.Rem1_10_2Remark 1.10.2
Record

The computation of Theorem 1.10 is viewed as a derivative in the F_l^* direction, corresponding under the analogy with p-adic Teichmueller theory ([pOrd], [pTeich]) to the derivative of the canonical Frobenius lifting. In [HASurII], Corollary 3.6, a portion of the arithmetic Kodaira-Spencer morphism coincides with the geometric one; in terms of the action of GL_2(F_l) on l-torsion this portion is given by the unipotent matrices, whereas the F_l^*-symmetries of the present papers correspond to the toral (diagonal) matrices. For large l, GL_2(F_l) is a good approximation of GL_2(Z) or GL_2(R), where toral subgroups correspond to isotropy subgroups (isomorphic to S^1) of points of the upper half-plane, a group-theoretic representation of tangent vectors.

Explicit hypotheses.

  • the notation of Theorem 1.10

Conclusion.

An analogy: the computation of Theorem 1.10 is a derivative in the F_l^-direction; F_l^-symmetries correspond to toral matrices of GL_2(F_l), in contrast with the unipotent matrices relevant to the arithmetic Kodaira-Spencer morphism of [HASurII]. No assertion needing proof.

Obligations.

  • Nothing to prove; a heuristic remark.

IUT4.Rem1_10_3Remark 1.10.3
Record

The terms involving l in the final display of Theorem 1.10 are presented as an inevitable consequence of the role of l-torsion points. It is said to be crucial to work over the field of rationality K of the l-torsion points (not over F) both for the global portions of the Theta NF- and Theta^{pm ell}-Hodge theaters and for their local portions (prime-strips), which are needed to glue these into a Theta^{pm ell} NF-Hodge theater; allowing any Galois indeterminacy on l-torsion points, even at v in V^good intersect V^non, would invalidate the manipulations of IUT I, sections 4 and 6.

Explicit hypotheses.

  • the notation of Theorem 1.10; K = F(E_F[l])

Conclusion.

An explanatory claim: working over K, including at the prime-strips at good nonarchimedean places, is necessary for the gluing of IUT I (Propositions 4.7, 6.5), and this produces the terms in l of Theorem 1.10. Stated without proof.

Obligations.

  • The claim that Galois indeterminacy at the l-torsion points would invalidate IUT I, sections 4 and 6, is asserted, not derived here.

IUT4.Rem1_10_4Remark 1.10.4
Record

The fluctuations of log-volume from the multiradial representation of IUT III Theorem 3.11 (i), computed in Theorem 1.10, are called inter-universal analytic torsion, analytic torsion being read as a metrized measure of the deviation of holomorphic functions from real analytic ones. Three cases: (a) in classical Arakelov theory, analytic torsion is the logarithm of a normalized determinant of a Laplacian, depending on the Kaehler metric and hence on the holomorphic moduli ([Arak]); (b) in scheme-theoretic Hodge-Arakelov theory, the comparison isomorphism of [HASurI] Theorem A and its Gaussian poles measure a discrepancy of integral structures near infinity, an analytic torsion at the divisor at infinity; (c) in IUT, the fluctuations come from comparing an alien arithmetic holomorphic structure with the multiradial representation, the object compared being values of the theta function. The terms involving the different d^K are called differential poles, and the prime number theorem (the Riemann zeta function) plays the role of normalized determinants.

Explicit hypotheses.

  • the notation of Theorem 1.10 and IUTchIII Theorem 3.11

Conclusion.

A terminological analogy: the log-volume fluctuations of Theorem 1.10 are a sort of inter-universal analytic torsion; the different terms are differential poles. No assertion needing proof.

Obligations.

  • Nothing to prove; a heuristic remark.

IUT4.Rem1_10_5Remark 1.10.5
Record

Computational aspects. (i) Unlike Corollaries 2.2 (ii) and 2.3, the inequalities of Theorem 1.10 have essentially explicit constants and exclude no non-explicit finite set of exceptional elliptic curves, so they suit explicit diophantine computations (for instance Fermat equations), which are not carried out. (ii) Asymptotics: for F_tpd = Q (d_mod = 1) and delta = log(d^{F_tpd}) + log(f^{F_tpd}) = log(f^{F_tpd}), the first bound of the final display of Theorem 1.10 has the form delta + * delta/l + * l + * with fixed positive constants *; the leading term is delta, and the epsilon terms * delta/l + * l are always >= * delta^{1/2} however l is chosen (take l ~ delta^alpha). This is compared with examples of abc sums of Masser and others ([Mss], [vFr] section 2, Equation (6)) whose left side exceeds delta + * delta^{1/2}/log(delta), and with an expectation of van Frankenhuijsen. The paper obtains epsilon terms of order * delta^{1/2} log(delta) under the assumption that the abc sums are compactly bounded away from infinity at 2 and at the archimedean prime (Corollary 2.2 (ii), Remark 2.2.1). (iii) The * l part of the epsilon terms comes from log(s^<=) in Step (viii), which roughly counts prime factors of abc that are <= e*_mod l, related to omega(abc) of [vFr] section 3 and reminiscent of Baker's refinements; examples of [vFr] section 3 Remark 1 with large omega(abc) fit the lower bound of (ii), while sums 2^n = p + q r (p, q, r primes) have omega(abc) <= 4 and left side about half the leading term.

Explicit hypotheses.

  • for (ii): F_tpd = Q, so d_mod = 1; delta = log(f^{F_tpd})

Implicit hypotheses.

  • the constants * in (ii) are fixed positive reals, independent of the initial Theta-data

Conclusion.

(i) The bounds of Theorem 1.10 are effective in form; (ii) with F_tpd = Q the bound has the shape delta + * delta/l + * l + *, whose epsilon terms are >= * delta^{1/2} for every choice of l, consistent with known abc examples; the paper's own bounds on epsilon terms are of order * delta^{1/2} log(delta) under compact boundedness at 2 and infinity; (iii) the * l term comes from log(s^<=) of Step (viii).

Obligations.

  • The lower bound >= * delta^{1/2} for the epsilon terms is sketched (compare delta^alpha with delta^{1-alpha}), not proved; the asymptotic claims about the cited examples are taken from [vFr] and [Mss].

Ambiguities.

  • Page 34: in (ii) delta is defined as log(d^{F_tpd}) + log(f^{F_tpd}) = log(f^{F_tpd}); with F_tpd = Q this uses that the different of Q is trivial.

IUT4.Rem1_10_6Remark 1.10.6
Record

(i) The bound on (1/6) log(q) of Theorem 1.10 concerns only the q-parameters at nonarchimedean places of V_mod^bad, all of odd residue characteristic (IUT I Definition 3.1 (b)); for the [Mss] examples it is not clear how to control the power of 2, but A. Venkatesh pointed out that those examples can be modified to give similar asymptotics without contributions at 2. (ii) Why places of even residue characteristic with bad multiplicative reduction are excluded from V_mod^bad: the theory depends on the etale theta function of [EtTh], which fails at primes over 2, through the simultaneous multiradiality of (1) constant multiple rigidity and (2) cyclotomic rigidity. Evaluating the theta series at the 2-torsion point in the irreducible component labeled zero gives a special value that is a unit for odd p but a nonzero non-unit for p = 2, so the integral structure (a) determined by that value coincides with the integral structure (b) given by the pole at the origin for odd p but not for p = 2; multiradiality of (1) needs (a), and working simultaneously with (b) violates the multiradiality of (2). (iii) It is not clear to the author how far (b) is needed; if (b) plays an essential role as well as (a), the theory is fundamentally incompatible with including even residue characteristic bad places in V_mod^bad. (iv) Classical theta functions and p-adic Teichmueller theory also behave differently or exclude the prime 2.

Explicit hypotheses.

  • the notation of Theorem 1.10 and IUTchI Definition 3.1

Conclusion.

Explanatory: the bound of Theorem 1.10 says nothing about q-parameters at places over 2; the exclusion of such places is attributed to the failure at p = 2 of the coincidence of the two integral structures (a), (b) on the theta function, and the author states that it is unclear whether (b) is necessary.

Obligations.

  • The unit versus non-unit computation of the special value at p = 2 is said to be easy but is not given; the incompatibility of the nontrivial denominator with multiradiality is asserted with references to IUT II.

Ambiguities.

  • Page 38, (iii): the author explicitly leaves open whether the integral structure (b) is necessary; the remark records an uncertainty of the source about its own framework at the prime 2.

(i) Since e*_mod <= d*_mod, one may replace e*_mod by d*_mod in the final two displays of the statement of Theorem 1.10. (ii) Within the framework of the series one cannot replace d_mod by e_mod in those displays: the multiradial representation of IUT III Theorem 3.11 (i) uses tensor products over Q of copies of F_mod labeled by j in F_l^* (IUT III Proposition 3.3), whose F_mod-linear structures cannot be identified for distinct labels since the tensor packets may depend only on the additive structure of the mono-analytic log-shells. Localizing at p therefore forces tensor products of localizations of F_mod at distinct primes over p; if one of them lies under a prime of K ramified over Q (condition (D5)), Step (v) produces a log(p) term in log(s^Q) from rounding up non-integral powers of p (Proposition 1.4 (iii)), since only integral powers of p make sense in the multiradial representation.

Explicit hypotheses.

  • the statement of Theorem 1.10; e*_mod <= d*_mod (since e_mod <= d_mod)

Implicit hypotheses.

  • the final inequality is monotone in e*_mod, the coefficient 20 l being positive

Conclusion.

(i) The final two displays of Theorem 1.10 remain true with d*_mod in place of e*_mod. (ii) Within the framework of the series, d_mod cannot be replaced by e_mod (an explanatory claim, not a theorem).

Obligations.

  • (i) follows from e*_mod <= d*_mod and monotonicity; not formalized as a separate lemma.
  • (ii) is an informal explanation of why the method gives d_mod, not a proof that e_mod is impossible.

      Record

      Over the fraction field of any discrete valuation ring, an integral Weierstrass equation whose discriminant or c4 has valuation 1 is minimal (Mathlib IsMinimal), and two minimal equations related by a change of variables have discriminants of the same valuation. For coprime a + b = c and an odd prime p, the Frey model y^2 = x(x - a)(x + b), base changed from Z to Q_p, is integral over Z_p and minimal at p: if p does not divide abc its discriminant 16(abc)^2 is a unit, otherwise its c4 = 16(a^2 + ab + b^2) is a unit.

      Explicit hypotheses.

      • a, b, c natural numbers with a + b = c and Nat.Coprime a b
      • p a prime ([Fact p.Prime]) with p != 2

      Conclusion.

      IsMinimal Z_p (freyRedModel p a b).

      Covers.

      The pages read do not name a triple, the Frey curve, its reduction at odd primes, or the relation v(q) = -v(j); this is classical arithmetic (Silverman) checked for the rational points a/c of the lambda-line coming from coprime triples, through the Frey curve y^2 = x(x - a)(x + b), a quadratic twist of the Legendre curve of page 41. It checks the minimality at odd primes on which the q-parameter orders at the primes not dividing 2 (log q^{not 2}, Corollary 2.2 (i), page 41) rest.

      Not covered.

      Number fields other than Q; points of the lambda-line not coming from triples; the Legendre model at lambda itself; the prime 2; every assertion of Corollary 2.2 (i), in particular the equalities of bounded discrepancy classes. Nothing is asserted for the Legendre model over Q at the point of the triple: minimality, reduction type, discriminant and conductor change under the quadratic twist relating it to the Frey curve. Counted as a model test: the pages read do not mention a triple, the Frey curve or its reduction; this is classical arithmetic behind the invariants of Corollary 2.2, as the record says.

      Ambiguities.

      • The paper works with q-parameters of curves over number fields; the identification with the Frey model over Q_p is the reader's specialization, not a statement of the paper.

IUT4.Rem2_2_1Remark 2.2.1
Record

(i) Asymptotics of the bound of Corollary 2.2 (ii) for F_tpd = Q (d_mod = 1), with h = log(q^forall) and delta = log-diff_X(x_E) + log-cond_D(x_E) = log-cond_D(x_E) (a notation different from the delta of Corollary 2.2 (ii)): since 1 < log 3 <= delta and 1 < log 3 <= h, the bound has the form (1/6) h <= delta + * delta^{1/2} log(delta) with a fixed positive *; h/delta is bounded below by definition and above by this bound. The epsilon term delta^{1/2} log(delta) is compared with interpretations of the Riemann hypothesis via weights (a height has the weight of one Tate twist, s = 1, so s = 1/2 corresponds to h^{1/2}, delta^{1/2}); the delta^{1/2} arises as a balance between the archimedean decrease delta/l and the nonarchimedean increase l of the epsilon terms (Steps (v), (viii); the b_i of Proposition 1.4 (iii); the radius of convergence of the p-adic logarithm in Proposition 1.2), likened to the functional equation of zeta. (ii) [vFr] section 2 conjectures limsup log((1/6) h - delta)/log(h) = 1/2; for abc sums in a fixed compactly bounded K_V the bounds of (i) imply limsup <= 1/2, while [vFr] shows limsup >= 1/2 for arbitrary abc sums; whether >= 1/2 holds inside a single K_V is unclear to the author. (iii) Hope for an inter-universal Mellin transform relating the theory to the Riemann zeta function. (iv) Function field analogy: the theory resembles the derivative of a Frobenius lifting, while the function field Riemann hypothesis uses the graph of Frobenius; perhaps an integral of the theory bears on the Riemann hypothesis for number fields. (v) Summary: the Riemann hypothesis inequality might be a restriction (ABC inequality)|_{canonical number} of an ABC inequality to a canonical number, an abstraction of sequences of abc sums, perhaps an average over all addition operations or an arithmetic measure analogous to the one giving the Mellin transform.

Explicit hypotheses.

  • for (i), (ii): the situation of Corollary 2.2 (ii) with F_tpd = Q (d_mod = 1); h = log(q^forall), delta = log-cond_D(x_E)

Implicit hypotheses.

  • * in (i) is a fixed positive real number, independent of x_E

Conclusion.

(i) Under F_tpd = Q, Corollary 2.2 (ii) yields (1/6) h <= delta + * delta^{1/2} log(delta) on K_V outside the exceptional set; (ii) consequently limsup log((1/6) h - delta)/log(h) <= 1/2 for abc sums in a fixed K_V; (iii) to (v) are speculative analogies with the Riemann zeta function and the Riemann hypothesis, not assertions.

Obligations.

  • The passage from (C2), with eps_E of order h^{-1/2} log(h), to the form delta + * delta^{1/2} log(delta) in (i) is stated without detail; it needs h and delta comparable, which (i) obtains from the bound itself.

Ambiguities.

  • Page 48: delta in this remark is log-cond_D(x_E) (log-diff_X vanishes when F_tpd = Q), not the delta = 2^12 3^3 5 d of Corollary 2.2 (ii); the remark warns of this.
  • Page 49, (ii): the claim limsup <= 1/2 is for abc sums in a single compactly bounded subset K_V; the remark does not state whether it holds for arbitrary abc sums.

IUT4.Rem2_2_2Remark 2.2.2
Record

On weights: the Gaussian integral int_{-infinity}^{infinity} e^{-x^2} dx = sqrt(pi) is viewed as a fundamental integral representation of a Tate semi-twist, while integral values of zeta and L-functions correspond to integral Tate twists, integral powers of 2 pi i (or of pi), the integral of d theta over S^1 equal to 2 pi, and G_m. Scheme-theoretic Hodge-Arakelov theory is a scheme-theoretic representation of a Tate semi-twist. (a) The Gaussian integral, (b) scheme-theoretic Hodge-Arakelov theory, (c) inter-universal Teichmueller theory and (d) the Riemann hypothesis are called phenomena of weight 1/2, the first three reflecting it in an exponential of a quadratic form, reminiscent of (1) Griffiths semi-transversality of the crystalline theta object, (2) the quadratic commutator of the theta group used in [EtTh], and (3) the quadratic nature of the epsilon term * delta/l + * l of Remark 1.10.5 (ii).

Conclusion.

A heuristic grouping of (a) to (d) as phenomena of weight 1/2; the only mathematical fact stated is the Gaussian integral value sqrt(pi) and the integral 2 pi of d theta over S^1.

Obligations.

  • Nothing to prove; a heuristic remark.

Ambiguities.

  • Page 51: 'fundamental scheme-theoretic represention' is a misprint for 'representation'.

IUT4.Rem2_2_4Remark 2.2.4
Record

Analogy with p-adic Teichmueller theory ([pOrd], [pTeich], [InpTch]). (i) The log-theta-lattice is compared with the canonical Frobenius lifting on the ordinary locus of a canonical curve over a perfect field; [pOrd] also treats the universal case over the moduli stack of hyperbolic curves with nilpotent ordinary indigenous bundles, smooth of dimension 3g - 3 + r over F_p and far from perfect. The gap between IUT and a canonical number (Remark 2.2.1 (v)) is likened to the gap between canonical curves and the non-perfect moduli stack: canonical number corresponds to modular Frobenius liftings. (ii) Non-perfectness reflects the failure of Frobenius to be an isomorphism; Frobenius corresponds to the log-link, and the * l term of Theorem 1.10 arises from the prime number theorem summing log-volumes of log-shells, which measure distortions of integral structures; l, of the order of the square root of the height by (C1), is a rough numerical representation of the moduli; these observations are said to support the view of (i). (iii) Modular Frobenius liftings live on a p-adic formal stack, not on the algebraic moduli stack; this gap is likened to the gap between compactly bounded subsets K_V (sufficiently general position, a global arithmetic ordinariness) and M_ell(Qbar), bridged in Corollary 2.3 by [GenEll] Theorem 2.1, an arithmetic analytic continuation by Belyi maps, and compared with the open immersion of [InpTch] section 2.6. (iv) The limit l -> infinity is the passage from the discrete approximation by l-torsion points to the full continuous theory, compared with Bernoulli numbers and the passage from f(x) -> f(x+1) - f(x) to d/dx, f(x+1) being e^{d/dx} f.

Conclusion.

A heuristic analogy: canonical number corresponds to modular Frobenius liftings; compactly bounded subsets correspond to ordinary loci; Corollary 2.3 via Belyi maps corresponds to analytic continuation; l -> infinity corresponds to the passage from difference to derivative operators. No assertion needing proof.

Obligations.

  • Nothing to prove; a heuristic remark.

IUT4.Cor2_3Corollary 2.3Diophantine Inequalities
Record

Diophantine inequalities: same statement as Theorem A. Proof: equivalent to [GenEll] Theorem 2.1 (i); by that theorem it suffices to prove (ii) of it, i.e. the inequality on K_V for the lambda-line, which follows from Corollary 2.2 (i), (ii), (iii) and d_mod <= d.

Explicit hypotheses.

  • X a smooth, proper, geometrically connected curve over a number field; D a reduced divisor; U_X = X minus D
  • d a positive integer, eps a positive real number
  • U_X hyperbolic: deg omega_X(D) > 0

Conclusion.

ht_{omega_X(D)} <~ (1 + eps)(log-diff_X + log-cond_D) on U_X(Qbar)^{<=d}, i.e. (1 + eps)(log-diff_X + log-cond_D) - ht_{omega_X(D)} is bounded below by a constant there.

Obligations.

  • Corollary 2.3 is not stated in Lean for general curves. Its instance X = P^1_Q, D = {0, 1, infinity} at points of every bounded degree is stated as an open proposition, with the height, log-different and log-conductor of [GenEll] Definition 1.5 defined from Mathlib objects (IUT4.Cor2_3.frag.bounded_degree_P1_minus_three); its degree one piece is the rational case IUT4.Cor2_3.frag.rational_points_P1_minus_three. In both, Mathlib's logarithmic height stands for the height attached to omega_X(D) (their agreement up to a bounded function is not formalized). The compactly bounded form of [GenEll] Theorem 2.1 (ii) and the reduced form of page 55 are stated as open propositions (GENELL.Thm2_1.frag.genell_ii_compactly_bounded, IUT4.Cor2_3.frag.reduced_form_j_inv); general curves and the proof are open.
  • [GenEll] Theorem 2.1 (the reduction to the lambda-line) is external; its direction (i) implies (ii) is proved for the instance (P, C) of (i) (GENELL.Thm2_1.frag.genell_i_implies_ii), and the direction (ii) implies (i) is not formalized. The proof derives its form (ii), on compactly bounded subsets; the special case of IUT4.Cor2_3.frag.rational_points_P1_minus_three is an instance of its form (i), so reaching it needs the direction (ii) implies (i), whose proof uses points of bounded degree over number fields and a noncritical Belyi map.
  • The fragments check only the logical form of the last step on K_V, as abstract lemmas on real functions on an arbitrary set.

Ambiguities.

  • Corollary 2.2 (iii) assumes epsilon <= 1; for epsilon > 1 the statement follows from epsilon = 1 since log-diff + log-cond >= 0 (BDle_mono_eps).

IUT4.Rem2_3_2Remark 2.3.2
Record

(i) Stronger versions of the estimates of Theorem 1.10 and Corollaries 2.2, 2.3 can be obtained with more care, but are not pursued. (ii) The constant 1 in the display of Corollary 2.3 cannot be improved (examples of [Mss]; Remark 1.10.5 (ii), (iii)). This is related to the breakdown of the theory if the first power of the etale theta function is replaced by an N-th power, N >= 2 (Step (xi) of the proof of IUT III Corollary 3.12; IUT III Remark 3.12.1 (ii)), which corresponds to replacing each Tate curve at V^bad by the Tate curve with N-th power q-parameter, an isogeny as in [GenEll] Lemma 3.5; the proof of that lemma shows the global height is essentially unchanged, up to a small discrepancy, under such isogenies, an invariance that is also essential in [Falt].

Explicit hypotheses.

  • the statement of Corollary 2.3

Conclusion.

(i) Stronger estimates are possible but not given. (ii) The factor 1 multiplying (log-diff_X + log-cond_D) in Corollary 2.3 cannot be replaced by a smaller constant, by the examples of [Mss]; the remark links this to the failure of the theory for N-th powers of the etale theta function and to invariance of heights under isogeny.

Obligations.

  • (ii), the optimality of the constant 1, rests on the examples of [Mss], which are not reproduced; (i) is unsubstantiated by design.

Corollary 2.3 is an effective version of the Mordell conjecture; the remark compares the ingredients of its proof (in effect, of the whole series) with those of [Falt] (discussions with I. Fesenko, summer 2015). (i) A rough list for [Falt]: (a) geometry of numbers, heights, Hermite-Minkowski; (b) global class field theory, dissected following [Lang1] (Weber's approach) into (b-1) local class field theory, (b-2) global density of primes (universal norm index inequality), (b-3) geometry of numbers giving the unit theorem, (b-4) global reciprocity (existence of a conductor for the Artin symbol), (b-5) Kummer theory; (c) p-adic Hodge-Tate decompositions; (d) finite flat group schemes; (e) isogenies and Tate modules; (f) polarizations; (g) logarithmic geometry of toroidal compactifications. (ii) Each is matched with an aspect of IUT: (a), (b-3) with nonzero global integers being roots of unity and with arithmetic degrees and global realified Frobenioids; (b-1) with p-adic absolute anabelian geometry; (b-2) with the prime number theorem (Propositions 1.6, 2.1 (ii)); (b-4) with Q_{>0} intersect Zhat^x = {1} in cyclotomic rigidity; (b-5) with Kummer theory; (c) with [pGC]; (d) with ramification computations for log-shells (Propositions 1.1 to 1.4); (e), (f) with finite etale coverings, Belyi maps, and commutators of theta groups; (g) with combinatorial anabelian geometry. (iii) Summary: aspects of [Falt] are distant abelian, arithmetically holomorphic ancestors of the anabelian, multiradial, mono-analytic theory of IUT; under arithmetic holomorphic structure a Frobenius morphism on a number field (multiplying arithmetic degrees by a factor > 1) cannot exist, while IUT asserts that one can be constructed canonically after dismantling that structure. (iv) The difference is mirrored by global density of primes versus the prime number theorem, which treats primes one by one. (v) Global reciprocity relates local units and local value groups at distinct primes, incompatible with the splittings used in IUT (prime-strips). (vi) Kummer-theoretic isomorphisms are strongly covariantly functorial, while reciprocity maps are not and are ill-suited to evaluating special functions at special points; the price in IUT is the nontrivial cyclotomic rigidity algorithms; local class field theory gives only uniradial algorithms. (vii) Comparison with Kronecker's Jugendtraum and Hilbert's twelfth problem and [Pano]; the author suggests the ideas of IUT resemble late nineteenth and early twentieth century mathematics, and that the course of later mathematics was one possible choice among many.

Conclusion.

An informal comparison of the ingredients of [Falt] with those of IUT, organized as (i) to (vii); its one substantive claim, that Corollary 2.3 is an effective version of the Mordell conjecture, is stated without argument, and the author disclaims completeness or rigor of the list.

Obligations.

  • The sense in which Corollary 2.3 is an effective Mordell conjecture (via [GenEll] and Belyi maps) is not explained here; the remainder is a heuristic comparison with nothing to prove.

IUT4.Rem2_3_5Remark 2.3.5
Record

[Par] proves the Mordell conjecture over complex function fields by metric estimates of displacements under the fundamental group of the base. Question (F. Voloch, September 2015): can part of IUT give a proof of Mordell over number fields without Belyi maps, as used in Corollary 2.3 via [GenEll] Theorem 2.1? The author's answer, as far as he can see, is no. (i) Starting from the Schwarz lemma and Kobayashi distance ([Lang2] Chapter I): (PB1) Parshin's proof uses the holomorphic (Kobayashi, Schwarz-theoretic) geometry of a two-dimensional complete hyperbolic manifold, Bogomolov's the real analytic symplectic geometry of the upper half-plane acting on a universal cover of S^1; this gap parallels the arithmetically holomorphic [Falt] versus the arithmetically quasi-conformal IUT (Remark 2.3.3 (iii)), so expecting a new Mordell proof from IUT is called unnatural. (ii) (PB2) Parshin uses many holomorphic maps from the disc D, Bogomolov a fixed copy of D; (PB3) Parshin's method gives rough finiteness for any genus >= 2, Bogomolov's explicit inequalities for elliptic curves; (PB4) Bogomolov's estimates depend on unipotent elements or commutators, Parshin's are uniform in small elements. (iii) The Schwarz-theoretic geometry of D has a natural analogue in IUT via categories of localizations ([GeoAnbd], [AbsTopI], [AbsTopII]), culminating in Belyi cuspidalizations: Belyi maps play the role of arithmetic analytic continuation. Hence any search in IUT for a Mordell proof or an analogue of Parshin's proof appears to lead to some application of Belyi maps.

Conclusion.

A negative heuristic answer: within IUT, a proof of the Mordell conjecture over number fields avoiding Belyi maps does not appear possible to the author; supported by the contrasts (PB1) to (PB4) and the role of Belyi maps as arithmetic analytic continuation. Not a theorem.

Obligations.

  • Nothing to prove; the answer 'no' is the author's assessment, explicitly qualified 'as far as the author can see'.

Ambiguities.

  • Page 65: 'applied to obtained' is a misprint for 'applied to obtain'.

IUT4.Rem3_1_1Remark 3.1.1
Record

Familiar descriptions of N (for instance [Drk] Chapter 2, Definitions 2.3, 2.9), Z, Q, Q_p or R yield species whose only species-morphisms are identities and which have a unique species-object in each ZFC-model. These differ from, for instance, the species of monoids isomorphic to N with monoid isomorphisms, which has many species-objects in any ZFC-model, all species-isomorphic. The set-theoretic formula defining the former species N may be used to define a model-free species-object N of the latter species.

Explicit hypotheses.

  • the descriptions of N, Z, Q, Q_p, R as set-theoretic formulas

Conclusion.

The species N, Z, Q, Q_p, R (with identity morphisms only) have exactly one species-object per ZFC-model; the species of monoids isomorphic to N has many species-objects, all species-isomorphic; the description of N gives a model-free species-object of the latter. Stated without proof.

Obligations.

  • Uniqueness of the species-object in each ZFC-model and model-freeness of the description of N are asserted, not checked.

IUT4.Rem3_1_2Remark 3.1.2
Record

(i) The essence of a species lies in its set-theoretic formulas (programs, software, a deterministic algorithm in a term suggested by Minhyong Kim), not in the sets occurring in particular ZFC-models. (ii) Analogy (from discussions with F. Kato): a fixed model of set theory is to the species-theoretic approach as varieties are to schemes, and as groups of specific matrices are to abstract groups; the category of a species in a ZFC-model is a specific representation of an abstract species. (iii) Identifying programs with the same output leads to an indeterminacy up to internal modifications of programs, with intractable problems beyond the scope of the paper.

Conclusion.

Heuristic explanation of the notion of species; no assertion needing proof.

Obligations.

  • Nothing to prove; an explanatory remark.

IUT4.Rem3_1_3Remark 3.1.3
Record

(i) The set-theoretic formulas of a species are usually not written out; they are those of the conventional descriptions of the objects, and one must check these are well defined and do not depend on arbitrary choices not describable by set-theoretic formulas. (ii) Data given by set-theoretic formulas carry a canonicality not shared by objects constructed using the axiom of choice in a particular ZFC-model; species thus let one measure the deviation of non-canonical objects from a canonical norm.

Conclusion.

A convention: the formulas are the conventional ones, subject to a well-definedness and choice-independence check by the reader; and a heuristic on canonicality.

Obligations.

  • The check that conventional descriptions are well defined and choice-free is delegated to the reader; it is not carried out for the species used in IUT.

Ambiguities.

  • Page 71: no criterion is given for when a construction counts as depending on 'arbitrary choices that are not describable via well-defined set-theoretic formulas'.

Since a species is given by set-theoretic formulas, the notion it defines is unaffected by extensions of the universe, such as the ascending chain V_0 in V_1 in ... in V of page 67. This is the sense of the term inter-universal: inter-universal geometry relates geometries occurring in distinct universes.

Explicit hypotheses.

  • set-theoretic formulas absolute in the sense of page 68

Conclusion.

A species is immune to extensions of the universe; this explains the term 'inter-universal'. The immunity rests on the absoluteness convention of page 68.

Obligations.

  • The immunity is a consequence of the absoluteness assumption of page 68, not proved independently.

IUT4.Ex3_2Example 3.2Categories
Record

Small categories, with isomorphism classes of covariant functors as morphisms, form a species: a category as a set of arrows with composition relations satisfying properties; a functor as the graph of its map on arrows; an isomorphism class of functors as a collection of such graphs. Dictionaries: 0-species with the notion of category, 1-species with the notion of isomorphism class of functors; 0-specimen with a particular small category, 1-specimen with a particular isomorphism class of functors.

Explicit hypotheses.

  • small categories; covariant functors considered up to isomorphism

Conclusion.

The notions of small category and isomorphism class of functors form a species, and species-isomorphisms between its species-objects correspond to isomorphism classes of equivalences of categories (stated as easily verified).

Obligations.

  • The set-theoretic formulas are written out in an arrows-only encoding and satisfy the absoluteness proviso of page 68 (IUT4.Ex3_2.frag.sa_cat_species). Not proved: that they satisfy conditions (c) to (e) of a species in every model (that composition of isomorphism classes of functors is well defined), and that species-isomorphisms are exactly isomorphism classes of equivalences of categories; the page asserts both as easily verified.

Ambiguities.

  • Page 72: the sentence speaks of 'species-isomorphisms between 0-species'; it is read as species-isomorphisms between species-objects (0-specimens), i.e. between categories.

IUT4.Rem3_2_1Remark 3.2.1
Record

In Example 3.2 one could define 2-species and 2-specimens using isomorphisms of functors and take functors (not isomorphism classes) as the 1-species, and more generally n-species for n >= 1; this is not done because it would add unnecessary complexity, so functors are taken up to isomorphism.

Conclusion.

A design choice: species are truncated at level 1, with functors up to isomorphism; higher n-species are possible but not used.

Obligations.

  • Nothing to prove.

IUT4.Def3_3Definition 3.3
Record

Mutations between species S, S': set-theoretic formulas Psi_0, Psi_1 assigning to each specimen of S a unique specimen of S', compatible with composites and identities (so a functor in every ZFC-model); morphisms of mutations (natural transformations), isomorphisms, mutation-equivalences and quasi-inverses; mutation-histories indexed by oriented graphs; covariant and contravariant observables of a mutation-history over a simply connected graph, and cores.

Explicit hypotheses.

  • S = (S_0, S_1) and S' = (S'_0, S'_1) species (Definition 3.1)
  • (ii): mutations M, M' : S ~> S'
  • (iii): a mutation M : S ~> S'; for the bijection statement, S and S' 1-small
  • (iv): an oriented graph (underlying graph with a total order on the branches of each edge)
  • (v): a mutation-history H whose underlying graph is simply connected, and a species S'

Conclusion.

Definitions of mutations, composition and identity mutations, morphisms and isomorphisms of mutations, mutation-equivalences (with the observation that for 1-small species they induce bijections on species-morphisms and species-isomorphisms), mutation-histories, observables and cores.

Obligations.

  • A definition: nothing to prove, except the observation in (iii). Mutations are defined in IUT.PaperIV.Species (IUT4.Def3_3.i.frag.mutation); the composite of two mutations between species is a mutation for the composite with the conditions on the source species added (IUT4.Def3_3.frag.sa_mutation_comp).

    Record

    A mutation M : S ~> S' between species is a pair of set-theoretic formulas: (a) Psi_0(E, E') in species-data for S_0 and S'_0, such that for each E in S_0 in a ZFC-model there is a unique E' in S'_0 with Psi_0(E, E'), written M(E); (b) Psi_1(E, E', F, F') such that for each species-morphism F : E -> E' of S there is a unique F' : M(E) -> M(E') of S' with Psi_1, written M(F); F -> M(F) must respect composites and identities. In a fixed ZFC-model, M determines a functor between the categories determined by S and S'. Composition and identity mutations are evident.

    Explicit hypotheses.

    • S = (S_0, S_1), S' = (S'_0, S'_1) species

    Conclusion.

    Definition of mutation, with the consequence that in each ZFC-model a mutation gives a functor; composition and identity mutations.

    Obligations.

    • A definition; that M is a functor in each ZFC-model is immediate. Mutations are defined in IUT.PaperIV.Species (IUT4.Def3_3.i.frag.mutation). That the composite of two mutations between species is a mutation is proved for the composite whose object formula carries Phi_0(E) and whose morphism formula carries Phi_0(E), Phi_0(E'), Phi_1(E, E', F) (IUT4.Def3_3.frag.sa_mutation_comp); it agrees with mutationAfter of IUT.PaperIV.Species on species-objects and species-morphisms of the source species.     Record

    A morphism of mutations Z : M -> M' (M, M' : S ~> S') is a set-theoretic formula Xi(E, F') such that for each species-object E of S there is a unique F' : M(E) -> M'(E) of S' with Xi, written Z(E), and for every species-morphism F : E_1 -> E_2 of S, M'(F) o Z(E_1) = Z(E_2) o M(F). In a fixed ZFC-model this is a natural transformation. Composition and identities are evident. Z is an isomorphism of mutations if every Z(E) is a species-isomorphism; equivalently (verified immediately) Z has a two-sided inverse morphism of mutations.

    Explicit hypotheses.

    • M, M' : S ~> S' mutations

    Conclusion.

    Definitions of morphism of mutations, its composition and identities, isomorphism of mutations, with the assertion that Z is an isomorphism iff it has an inverse morphism of mutations.

IUT4.Rem3_3_1Remark 3.3.1
Record

(i) The axiom of foundation forbids membership loops a in b in c in ... in a, yet one often wishes to identify objects at higher and lower levels of the membership structure; sets and bijections allow this, and species extend it: species-isomorphisms between species-objects at different levels simulate membership loops without violating foundation, typically identifying output species-objects with input species-objects of a mutation-history ... ~> S ~> S' ~> S'' ~> ... ~> S ~> .... (ii) The simpler the species, the easier to build loops; hence categories (Example 3.2) are preferred to schemes, a principal motivation for the geometry of categories and absolute anabelian geometry ([MnLg], [SemiAnbd], [Cusp], [FrdI]), for instance reconstruction of the underlying scheme in [MnLg] via Definition 1.1 (iv), and slim exponentiation in the Appendix to [FrdI]. (iii) It is also of interest to consider the portions left unaltered by the mutations, hence cores; cores allow one to describe, by non-coric observables, the altered portions in terms of the unaltered ones (cf. Remark 3.6.1 (ii)).

Conclusion.

Heuristic motivation of species, mutation-histories and cores; no assertion needing proof.

Obligations.

  • Nothing to prove; an explanatory remark.

A naive original motivation: local systems on a scheme need not be valued in modules over a finite ring; one may take local systems of schemes (the Galois mantle of [pTeich]) or of more general collections of objects, then local systems on their fibers, and so on, leading to systems of nested local systems. This underlies successive iteration of a mutation-history; viewing such iterates as an abstraction of nested local systems, a core is an object invariant under the operations producing them.

Conclusion.

Heuristic motivation of iterated mutation-histories and cores; no assertion needing proof.

IUT4.Ex3_4Example 3.4Topological Spaces and Fundamental Groups
Record

(i) Topological spaces with continuous maps form a species S^top; universal coverings Xt -> X of pathwise connected spaces with compatible pairs of continuous maps considered up to deck transformations of the target covering form a species S^{u-top}, whose species-morphisms are, set-theoretically, collections of continuous maps differing by deck transformations. (ii) Groups with outer homomorphisms (homomorphisms up to inner automorphisms of the codomain) form a species S^gp, whose species-morphisms are collections of homomorphisms differing by inner automorphisms. (iii) The assignment (Xt -> X) -> Aut(Xt/X) (the deck transformation group) is a mutation S^{u-top} ~> S^gp: the fundamental group is a mutation.

Explicit hypotheses.

  • (i): pathwise connected topological spaces with universal coverings
  • (ii): groups and outer homomorphisms

Conclusion.

(i) S^top and S^{u-top} are species; (ii) S^gp is a species; (iii) Xt -> X maps to Aut(Xt/X) is a mutation S^{u-top} ~> S^gp. All stated as easily verified, with the set-theoretic formulas left to the reader.

Obligations.

  • The set-theoretic formulas and the verification that (iii) respects composites and identities (an outer homomorphism of deck groups for each morphism of coverings up to deck transformations) are left to the reader.

IUT4.Ex3_5Example 3.5Absolute Anabelian Geometry
Record

(i) For a class S of connected normal schemes closed under isomorphism, with a set E_S describable by a set-theoretic formula containing a representative of every isomorphism class, universal pro-finite etale coverings of schemes in S with isomorphisms up to deck transformations form a species S^S. (ii) Likewise, for a class G of topological groups closed under isomorphism with such a set E_G, the groups of G with bicontinuous outer isomorphisms form a species S^G. (iii) For suitable G, deck transformation groups give a mutation Pi : S^S ~> S^G; the schemes of S may be called [absolute] anabelian if one specifies a mutation A : S^G ~> S^S that is a mutation-quasi-inverse of Pi. The existence of the bijections (full faithfulness) of Definition 3.3 (iii) is essentially the usual definition of anabelian; the species-theoretic approach formulates the algorithmic approach of [AbsTopI]. (iv) One must specify which species one works with: a profinite group merely as a profinite group differs substantially from the same group equipped with data from its construction as an etale fundamental group; this issue was a motivation for the theory of species.

Explicit hypotheses.

  • (i): S a class of connected normal schemes closed under isomorphism, with a set E_S given by a set-theoretic formula meeting every isomorphism class
  • (ii): G a class of topological groups closed under isomorphism, with a set E_G given by a set-theoretic formula meeting every isomorphism class
  • (iii): G chosen appropriately

Conclusion.

(i) S^S and (ii) S^G are species; (iii) Pi : S^S ~> S^G is a mutation, and 'anabelian' is defined by the specification of a mutation-quasi-inverse A of Pi; (iv) a heuristic on specifying species.

Obligations.

  • (i) to (iii) are stated as easily verified; the 'appropriate choice of G' in (iii) is not specified.
  • No anabelian result is proved here; (iii) is a definition.

Ambiguities.

  • Page 77, (iii): 'an appropriate choice of G' is left unspecified; it must at least contain the deck groups of the coverings in S.

IUT4.Ex3_6Example 3.6The Étale Site and Frobenius
Record

(i) For a prime p and a reduced scheme S over F_p, S^(p) has the topological space of S and structure sheaf O_S^p; the inclusion gives Phi_S : S -> S^(p), and p-th powers give a natural isomorphism alpha_S : S^(p) -> S with alpha_S o Phi_S the Frobenius of S. S^{p-sch} is the species of reduced quasi-compact schemes over F_p with quasi-compact morphisms. The small etale site S_et has as objects etale morphisms of finite presentation T -> S equipped with a finite open cover {U_i} of S and factorizations T|_{U_i} in A^{N_i}_{U_i} -> U_i exhibiting finitely presented subschemes (every such T admits these data), and S-morphisms as arrows. S -> S_et is contravariantly functorial and given by set-theoretic formulas, giving the etale site mutation M^et : S^{p-sch} ~> S^cat (S^cat: categories with isomorphism classes of contravariant functors). The perfection S^pf (inverse limit of iterated Frobenius) with beta_S : S^pf -> S gives the perfection mutation M^pf : S^{p-sch} ~> S^{p-sch}. (ii) The Frobenius mutation F^{p-sch} : S -> S^(p) defines the Frobenius mutation-history ... ~> S^{p-sch} ~> S^{p-sch} ~> ...; invariance of the etale site under Frobenius ([FK] Chapter I, Proposition 3.16) says M^et exhibits S^cat as a core; M^pf also gives a core; Phi_S is a covariant observable with identity observation mutations, non-coric since Phi_S is not in general an isomorphism; beta_S is a morphism of mutations M^pf -> id relating it to the coric observable of M^pf. (iii) For torsion-free abelian monoids S^mon, M -> M^(p) = p M is the monoid-Frobenius mutation F^mon, with monoid-Frobenius mutation-history and a non-coric contravariant observable given by the inclusions M^(p) -> M; the p-perfection M^pf (inductive limit of multiplication by p) gives a core M^{pf-mon}, and M -> M^pf is a morphism of mutations id -> M^{pf-mon} relating the two.

Explicit hypotheses.

  • (i): p a prime; S a reduced scheme over F_p; for the species S^{p-sch}, reduced quasi-compact schemes over F_p and quasi-compact morphisms
  • (iii): S^mon the species of torsion-free abelian monoids and monoid morphisms

Conclusion.

(i) Definitions of S^(p), Phi_S, alpha_S, S_et and the mutations M^et, M^pf; (ii) by [FK] Chapter I, Proposition 3.16, M^et is a core of the Frobenius mutation-history, M^pf is a core, Phi_S is a non-coric covariant observable related to M^pf by beta_S; (iii) the monoid analogue, with a non-coric contravariant observable and the core M^{pf-mon}.

Obligations.

  • That S -> S_et and S -> S^pf are given by set-theoretic formulas and are functorial is asserted; the coricity of M^et rests on [FK] Chapter I, Proposition 3.16, and the coricity of M^pf and M^{pf-mon} on the evident identifications S^pf = (S^(p))^pf, which are not written out.
  • (iii) for log schemes is left to the reader.

IUT4.Rem3_6_2Remark 3.6.2
Record

(i) Coric descriptions of non-coric data must use set-theoretic formulas: descriptions using arbitrary choices depending on a model of set theory do not allow one to calculate, within one universe, operations performed in an alien universe, as happens for the arrows of the log-theta-lattice, where distinct universes arise from distinct scheme-theoretic basepoints of ring theories not related by ring homomorphisms; this need led to inter-universal Teichmueller theory. The algorithmic approach (as opposed to a fully faithful, Grothendieck conjecture style approach, Example 3.5 (iii)) is essential, since only specific algorithms reveal relations between components, e.g. the cyclotomic rigidity isomorphisms behind Theta^{x mu}_LGP-link compatibility ([IUTchIII] Theorem 3.11 (iii) (c), (d)). (ii) The algorithmic approach of the series ([FrdI], [EtTh], [AbsTopIII]) was conceived in the spirit of species; the formulas are left implicit and the reader must check that conventional descriptions are well defined and choice-free. (iii) Cataloguing the possibilities arising from choices leads to sets of very large cardinality built by set-theoretic exponentiation (E -> 2^E), reminiscent of the growth of denominators when integrating an arbitrary connection in p-adic crystalline theory, as opposed to canonical connections and canonical liftings ([pOrd], [pTeich]), which may be liftings of minimal complexity ([Finot]).

Conclusion.

Heuristic: set-theoretic formulas and specific algorithms are needed to compare constructions across universes; the reader must check that the series' conventional descriptions are choice-free. No assertion needing proof.

Obligations.

  • Page 82, (ii): the verification that the conventional descriptions used throughout IUT are well defined and independent of arbitrary choices is explicitly left to the reader; this is an open obligation for any formalization of IUT I to III.

IUT4.Rem3_6_3Remark 3.6.3
Record

(i) The fundamental reason for inter-universality ([IUTchIII] Remarks 1.2.4, 1.4.2): etale fundamental groups (Galois groups) are automorphism groups of rings, which is incompatible with the vertical and horizontal arrows of the log-theta-lattice, as these do not arise from ring homomorphisms. Hence for v in V^non the only natural correspondence describable by set-theoretic formulas between the isomorphs of G_v on either side of a vertical or horizontal arrow is an indeterminate isomorphism of topological groups, and for Delta_v = Ker(Pi_v -> G_v) across a vertical (not horizontal) arrow an indeterminate isomorphism equipped with an outer action of G_v. (ii) For v in V^bad: (V1) across a vertical arrow the full arithmetic fundamental groups Pi_v are identified up to isomorphism; (H1) across a horizontal arrow only the G_v are identified and the Delta_v are distinguished. Reasons: (V2) constructing the log-link (the p_v-adic logarithm power series) needs the local ring structures, reconstructible only from the full Pi_v; (H2) constructing the Theta^{x mu}_gau, Theta^{x mu}_LGP, Theta^{x mu}_lgp-links, i.e. q -> {q^{j^2}}_{j = 1, ..., l*}, needs an isomorphism between objects depending on the labels j (built from Delta_v) and a label-free object q, possible only if the Delta_v on the two sides are kept distinct. The simultaneous realization of label-dependent and label-free objects in (H2) is likened to the vertical bicoricity of [IUTchIII] Theorem 1.5.

Explicit hypotheses.

  • the notation of IUTchI Definition 3.1 (e), (f); v in V^non (for (i)) or v in V^bad (for (ii))

Conclusion.

Explanatory claims: (i) across arrows of the log-theta-lattice only indeterminate isomorphisms of G_v (and of Delta_v with outer action, across vertical arrows) are describable by set-theoretic formulas; (ii) (V1)/(V2) and (H1)/(H2) explain why vertical arrows identify Pi_v and horizontal arrows only G_v. Stated as consequences of the constructions of IUT I to III, not proved here.

Obligations.

  • The claims that the indeterminate isomorphisms are the only natural correspondences describable by set-theoretic formulas, and the necessity statements in (V2) and (H2), are asserted with references to IUT III; no proof is given here and none is formalized.

Ambiguities.

  • Page 83: 'the only natural correspondence' is not given a precise meaning; whether it is a uniqueness theorem or an informal assessment is not specified. This concerns the much-discussed identifications across Theta-links in IUT III.

A topological pseudo-monoid is a topological space P with a continuous map S → P, S ⊆ P × P, such that there are a topological abelian group M (written multiplicatively) and an embedding ι : P ↪ M with S = {(a, b) | ι(a)·ι(b) ∈ ι(P)} and S → P the restriction of the group law. For a topological group Π, B^temp(Π) is the category of countable discrete sets with continuous Π-action and Π-equivariant maps. IUT1.Sec0.Valuationsdefinition
Record

NF, MLF, CAF abbreviate number field, mixed-characteristic nonarchimedean local field, complex archimedean field; Primes is the set of prime numbers. For a number field F, V(F) = V(F)^arc ∪ V(F)^non is the set of valuations (places) of F; F_v is the completion at v; an element is integral at v if of norm ≤ 1; for a Galois extension L of F, L_v is the completion at a valuation of L over v; p_v is the residue characteristic for nonarchimedean v and, for archimedean v, the positive real element of F_v with natural logarithm 1 (p_v = e). These notations extend to infinite extensions of Q by projective or inductive limits.

Conclusion.

Definition (no proof obligation).

IUT4.Sec3.Universesconvention
Record

Setting of Section 3: ZFC-models (models of the nine Zermelo-Fraenkel axioms and choice); a Grothendieck universe V is a set that is transitive, contains N, and is closed under power sets, unions of members, and images of surjections from members onto subsets of V; a V-set is an element of V. The ZFC-models used are typically those of universes inside an ambient ZFC-model satisfying the existence axiom (dagger^G): every set lies in some universe (a ZFCG-model). Consequence proved on page 67: for any set-indexed family of universes V_i there is a universe V with V_i in V for all i (apply (dagger^G) to the set {V_i} and use transitivity), so infinite ascending chains V_0 in V_1 in ... in V exist, while the axiom of foundation forbids infinite descending chains. Every set-theoretic formula used is assumed absolute: its validity for sets in a universe V is the same relative to V and to any universe W with V in W.

Explicit hypotheses.

  • an ambient ZFC-model satisfying the existence axiom (dagger^G)

Conclusion.

Definitions of ZFC-model, universe, V-set, ZFCG-model; the proposition that any set-indexed family of universes is contained (as elements) in one universe, hence infinite ascending chains of universes exist; the absoluteness convention for set-theoretic formulas.

Obligations.

  • The existence of ZFCG-models is not discussed; the paper defers to [Ffmn] and states that precise statements lie beyond its scope (page 68).
  • The absoluteness of every set-theoretic formula used is an assumption of the section, not verified for any particular formula.

Ambiguities.

  • Page 68: the absoluteness proviso is imposed globally on 'every set-theoretic formula that appears'; which formulas of Sections 1 to 2 or of IUT I to III are meant to satisfy it is not specified.

Pages read: renders of pages 67 and 68
